text.p: The following is a chronology of the attempts to sell Creditanstalt-Bankverein, Austria's longest running privatisation since World War Two.
1990 - The ruling coalition of Social Democrats and conservative People's Party agreed to put the state's 70 percent of Creditanstalt ordinary voting shares up for sale.
March 14, 1991 - Parliament stipulated the sale must safeguard Austrian interests.
April 30, 1993 - Austrian cooperative banking group Raiffeisen targeted a merger with Creditanstalt.
May 6, 1993 - Finance Minister Ferdinand Lacina turned down Raiffeisen after Creditanstalt's board opposed the plan.
January, 1994 - Switzerland's CS Holding emerged as a potential buyer.
March 16, 1994 - Austrian industrialists, including juice maker Rauch and carton board maker Mayr-Melnhof, began forming the "Austrian consortium". Insurer EA-Generali said it was keen join.
May 6, 1994 - Savings bank Die Erste Oesterreichische SparCasse Bank (First Austrian) joined the group, which received open support from Creditanstalt executives.
May 19, 1994 - CS Holding said it wanted to buy 20-30 percent of Creditanstalt shares at once, then take full control.
May 26, 1994 - The Austrian consortium, led by EA-Generali, offered 7.2 billion schillings ($651.6 million) for 37 percent of voting shares.
August 16, 1994 - Creditanstalt employees threatened mass resignations if the CS Holding bid succeeded.
September 12, 1994 - CS Holding, citing disillusionment with political in-fighting, dropped its bid.
January 19, 1995 - Germany's Allianz Holding AG and Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG submitted an offer for Creditanstalt.
March 14, 1995 - The Austrian consortium placed a fresh bid of 10 billion schillings for half the government's stake and proposed selling the rest through a secondary offering.
March 16, 1995 - Allianz and Bayerische Hypo withdrew, citing an unfair due-diligence process.
April 6, 1995 - Ferdinand Lacina resigned as finance minister, replaced by little-known accountant Andreas Staribacher.
July 14, 1995 - J.P. Morgan, hired as the government's adviser, valued the bank stake at 18 billion schillings, including a premium of six billion schillings for majority control.
September 7, 1995 - Austria invited new bids by October 9.
October 1995 - The coalition government collapsed and a new election was called, putting the Creditanstalt sale on ice.
December 18, 1995 - The Social Democrats again emerged as the strongest party in the vote.
January 2, 1996 - Staribacher resigned and was replaced by Transport Minister Viktor Klima.
June, 1996 - First Austrian proposed a holding company to control it and Creditanstalt, Creditanstalt executives reject the plan.
July 17, 1996 - Klima said the consortium must make a bid by the end of August or he would reopen the race.
September 2, 1996 - Klima extended deadline to September 6.

September 6, 1996 - First Austrian announced it had quit the consortium. The rest of the group, led by EA-Generali bid nine billion schillings for half the government's stake and proposed selling the remainder through a secondary offering.
September 23, 1996 - Klima rejected the group's bid because it was not for the entire stake, invited new bids by Nov 15.
November 13, 1996 - Die Erste rejoined the Austrian consortium led by EA-Generali, which confirmed it would make a new offer.
November 15, 1996 - Deadline for indicative offers expired.
November 20, 1996 - Media reports said the Austrian consortium had bid 720-730 schillings a share for two-thirds of the state's stake. Klima said he received two indicative offers.
December 11, 1996 - Bank Austria supervisory board voted to make an offer, but gave no details.
December 13, 1996 - Austrian parliament called on the government to reject Bank Austria's offer.
December 16, 1996 - Klima confirmed Bank Austria and EA-Generali led group's bids and a third bid by entrepreneur Karl Wlaschek.
December 27, 1996 - Finance ministry reopened tender to allow existing three bidders to improve their offers and set a new deadline on January 10.
January 8, 1997 - EA-Generali group raised its bid but gave no details.
January 9, 1997 - The coalition government agreed to convene for an emergency meeting of leaders on January 11 to discuss the political impasse surrounding the sale.
January 10, 1997 - The deadline for the final tender expired at 0800 GMT. Klima said he expected to make a decision on the sale before a special session of parliament on January 14.
Minutes before deadline ended, Bank Austria raised its bid but revealed no details. ($1=11.05 Schilling)
